subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He has a tall, slender build with disproportionately long arms and legs, gynecomastia, and a female-pattern pubic hair distribution. Testicular examination reveals small, firm testes. He reports mild learning difficulties in school.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: 47,XYY syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Turner syndrome (45,XO)
Androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY)
Kallmann syndrome

explanation_correct: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common cause of hypogonadism seen in the infertility workup. Dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules produces small, firm testes and azoospermia, while abnormal Leydig cell function lowers testosterone. Delayed epiphyseal closure leads to tall stature with eunuchoid proportions (long limbs), and increased estrogen relative to androgen causes gynecomastia and a female hair distribution. A Barr body is present because of the inactivated X chromosome, and there is an increased risk of breast cancer. Developmental delay may also occur.

explanation_incorrect.A: 47,XYY males are phenotypically normal, very tall, and have normal fertility and normal testes, not small firm testes with gynecomastia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Turner syndrome is 45,XO in a phenotypic female with short stature and streak ovaries; it does not occur in a male with testes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Androgen insensitivity produces a female-appearing 46,XY individual with breasts, female external genitalia, and no uterus, not a male with small firm testes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and failure of puberty, not gynecomastia with small firm testes after normal pubertal development.

educationalObjective: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes small firm testes, azoospermia, tall eunuchoid proportions, gynecomastia, and female hair distribution — the classic hypogonadism of the infertility workup.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A 28-year-old man with 47,XXY Klinefelter syndrome has small, firm testes and azoospermia. Laboratory testing is performed to evaluate his hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
question: Which of the following hormone patterns is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Increased inhibin B, decreased FSH, increased testosterone, decreased LH
Decreased inhibin B, decreased FSH, decreased testosterone, increased LH
Decreased inhibin B, increased FSH, decreased testosterone, increased LH
Increased inhibin B, increased FSH, increased testosterone, increased LH
Decreased inhibin B, increased FSH, increased testosterone, decreased LH

explanation_correct: In Klinefelter syndrome, dysgenesis of the seminiferous tubules reduces inhibin B secretion; because inhibin B normally provides negative feedback on FSH, FSH rises. Abnormal Leydig cell function decreases testosterone production, removing negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so LH rises. This hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism pattern of decreased inhibin B/increased FSH and decreased testosterone/increased LH is characteristic. The elevated LH also drives aromatization of androgens to estrogen, contributing to gynecomastia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Inhibin B is low, not high, in seminiferous tubule dysgenesis, so FSH should be elevated rather than suppressed; testosterone is also low, not high.
explanation_incorrect.B: With low inhibin B, FSH should be increased from loss of negative feedback, not decreased; the testosterone/LH portion is correct but FSH is wrong.
explanation_incorrect.D: Inhibin B and testosterone are both reduced in Klinefelter syndrome, not increased; only FSH and LH are elevated.
explanation_incorrect.E: Testosterone is low and LH is high in primary testicular failure; elevated testosterone with low LH suggests an androgen-secreting tumor or exogenous androgen use.

educationalObjective: Klinefelter syndrome produces primary hypogonadism: decreased inhibin B leads to increased FSH from seminiferous tubule dysgenesis, and decreased testosterone leads to increased LH from Leydig cell dysfunction.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and lack of breast development. She has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a webbed neck, and lymphedema of the hands and feet. Cardiac examination reveals a systolic murmur and weaker femoral than brachial pulses.
question: Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Streak ovaries with ovarian dysgenesis
Small, firm testes with azoospermia
A Barr body present on buccal smear
Virilized external genitalia with normal ovaries
Multiple cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules

explanation_correct: This is Turner syndrome (45,XO), the most common cause of primary amenorrhea. Ovarian dysgenesis produces streak ovaries (streak gonads) that fail to produce estrogen, leading to sexual infantilism and short stature (preventable with growth hormone therapy). Other classic features include a bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta with femoral pulses weaker than brachial pulses, webbed neck or cystic hygroma from lymphatic defects, horseshoe kidney, high-arched palate, and shortened fourth metacarpals. There is no Barr body because only one X chromosome is present.

explanation_incorrect.B: Small, firm testes with azoospermia are features of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) in a male, not Turner syndrome in a female.
explanation_incorrect.C: A Barr body reflects an inactivated X chromosome; Turner syndrome (45,XO) has no second X and therefore no Barr body. A Barr body is present in Klinefelter syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Virilized external genitalia with ovaries suggests 46,XX DSD (eg, congenital adrenal hyperplasia), not the phenotypic female with streak ovaries seen in Turner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules are features of neurofibromatosis type 1, not Turner syndrome.

educationalObjective: Turner syndrome (45,XO) is phenotypic female with short stature, streak ovaries, webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve/coarctation, and no Barr body — a classic cause of primary amenorrhea.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A 19-year-old woman with Turner syndrome (45,XO) presents with primary amenorrhea. She has never had a menstrual period and has no breast development. She has short stature and a webbed neck.
question: Which of the following best explains her amenorrhea and expected hormone levels?

options.text: Normal estrogen with elevated LH and FSH due to pituitary failure
Elevated estrogen with low LH and FSH due to an estrogen-secreting ovarian tumor
Normal estrogen and normal LH/FSH with an anatomic outflow tract obstruction
Decreased estrogen with elevated LH and FSH due to ovarian dysgenesis
Decreased estrogen with decreased LH and FSH due to hypothalamic dysfunction

explanation_correct: Turner syndrome causes ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries) that cannot produce estrogen. The loss of estrogen negative feedback leads to elevated LH and FSH, a hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism pattern. This is why Turner syndrome is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea; affected patients experience menopause before menarche. Short stature is due to haploinsufficiency and is partially preventable with growth hormone therapy; pregnancy is possible in some cases with in vitro fertilization using donor oocytes plus exogenous estradiol and progesterone.

explanation_incorrect.A: Estrogen is low, not normal, in Turner syndrome, and the pituitary is functioning normally; the elevated LH/FSH reflect loss of ovarian negative feedback, not pituitary failure.
explanation_incorrect.B: An estrogen-secreting tumor would suppress LH and FSH and cause breast development and uterine bleeding, the opposite of streak ovaries with primary amenorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.C: An outflow tract obstruction (eg, imperforate hymen) would cause cyclic pain with normal secondary sexual characteristics and normal hormones, not the hormone deficiency and absent breast development here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Low LH and FSH would indicate hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism; in Turner syndrome the gonadotropins are elevated because the defect is at the ovary. Haploinsufficiency, not hypothalamic dysfunction, is the cause.

educationalObjective: In Turner syndrome, streak ovaries lead to decreased estrogen and increased LH/FSH (hypergonadotropic primary hypogonadism), producing primary amenorrhea (menopause before menarche).

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: Genetic counseling is being provided to the parents of a girl with Turner syndrome. The counselor explains the mechanisms of sex chromosome loss and the implications of mosaicism.
question: Which of the following statements about the genetics of Turner syndrome is correct?

options.text: The missing X chromosome is always of maternal origin
A 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype is associated with a decreased risk of gonadoblastoma
Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization produces only 45,X cells in all tissues
Meiotic nondisjunction causing Turner syndrome most commonly involves maternal gametes
A 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype carries an increased risk of gonadoblastoma

explanation_correct: Aneuploidy most commonly results from meiotic nondisjunction. In Turner syndrome, sex chromosome (X or, rarely, Y) loss can occur during meiosis — usually in paternal gametes, producing sperm missing a sex chromosome — or during mitosis after zygote formation, producing mosaicism (eg, 45,X/46,XX). A 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype is associated with an increased risk of gonadoblastoma because of the Y chromosome material, so prophylactic gonadectomy is often considered. Meiotic errors in Turner syndrome are usually paternal, not maternal. Mitotic errors affect some but not all cells, yielding mosaicism rather than uniform 45,X in every tissue.

explanation_incorrect.A: The lost sex chromosome can be paternal or maternal; meiotic errors in Turner syndrome usually occur in paternal gametes, so 'always maternal' is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.B: It is the opposite — 45,X/46,XY mosaicism increases, not decreases, gonadoblastoma risk because Y chromosome material is present.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mitotic errors after zygote formation produce mosaicism (loss in some but not all cells), not 45,X in every tissue; uniform 45,X arises from meiotic errors or very early loss.
explanation_incorrect.D: Meiotic nondisjunction causing Turner syndrome usually occurs in paternal gametes (sperm missing the sex chromosome), not maternal gametes.

educationalObjective: Turner syndrome results from sex chromosome loss via meiotic nondisjunction (usually paternal) or postzygotic mitosis (mosaicism); 45,X/46,XY mosaicism raises gonadoblastoma risk.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A 22-year-old man is found to have a 47,XYY karyotype during evaluation of a learning disorder. He is tall, has normal male external genitalia and normal testicular size, and has fathered a child. He has a history of severe acne and features of autism spectrum disorder.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition?

options.text: Infertility due to azoospermia and small, firm testes
Normal male phenotype and fertility with tall stature and increased risk of learning disability
Female phenotype with breast development and absent uterus
Short stature with webbed neck and streak ovaries
Gynecomastia and female hair distribution with delayed epiphyseal closure

explanation_correct: Double Y males (47,XYY) are phenotypically normal, usually undiagnosed, and very tall. They have normal fertility and normal virilization, distinguishing them from Klinefelter syndrome. Associations include severe acne, learning disability, and autism spectrum disorders. The extra Y chromosome arises from meiotic nondisjunction (usually paternal meiosis II). There is no gynecomastia, azoospermia, or characteristic sex hormone abnormality in this karyotype.

explanation_incorrect.A: Azoospermia with small, firm testes is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY); 47,XYY males have normal testes and normal fertility.
explanation_incorrect.C: A female phenotype with breasts and absent uterus suggests androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), not a 47,XYY male.
explanation_incorrect.D: Short stature, webbed neck, and streak ovaries are features of Turner syndrome (45,XO), not a 47,XYY male.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gynecomastia, female hair distribution, and delayed epiphyseal closure with tall stature are features of Klinefelter syndrome, not 47,XYY.

educationalObjective: 47,XYY (double Y) males are phenotypically normal and fertile but very tall, with associations of severe acne, learning disability, and autism — unlike Klinefelter syndrome.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Sex chromosome disorders: Klinefelter, Turner, double Y
vignette: A genetics lecture reviews sex chromosome disorders and the application of the Barr body test. The lecturer emphasizes that the presence or absence of an inactivated X chromosome helps distinguish Klinefelter from Turner syndrome.
question: Which of the following statements regarding these disorders is correct?

options.text: A Barr body is present in Turner syndrome (45,XO)
Aneuploidy most commonly results from mitotic nondisjunction in somatic cells
A Barr body is present in Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) but absent in Turner syndrome (45,XO)
Klinefelter syndrome results from a missing X chromosome and is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea
A 47,XYY male has female hair distribution and gynecomastia

explanation_correct: A Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome; the number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one. Klinefelter males (47,XXY) have one inactivated X and therefore one Barr body, whereas Turner females (45,XO) have no second X and no Barr body. Aneuploidy most commonly arises from meiotic nondisjunction, not somatic mitosis. Klinefelter is a male with an extra X and causes hypogonadism in the infertility workup; Turner (missing X) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea. A 47,XYY male is a normal, fertile, very tall male without gynecomastia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Turner syndrome (45,XO) has no second X chromosome to inactivate, so no Barr body is present.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aneuploidy most commonly results from meiotic nondisjunction (eg, during gametogenesis), not mitotic nondisjunction in somatic cells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Klinefelter syndrome has an extra X (47,XXY) in a male and causes male hypogonadism; primary amenorrhea from a missing X is Turner syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: 47,XYY males are phenotypically normal with normal virilization and fertility; gynecomastia and female hair distribution are features of Klinefelter syndrome.

educationalObjective: Barr body equals the number of X chromosomes minus one: present in 47,XXY Klinefelter, absent in 45,XO Turner, and sex chromosome aneuploidy is usually due to meiotic nondisjunction.
